result.markdown: --- title: "Markov chain Monte Carlo" author: "Dr. Alexander Fisher" execute: warning: true format: revealjs: smaller: true --- ## Today By the end, you should be able to: 1. Explain why we might use a Markov chain for Monte Carlo simulation. 2. Describe the **Metropolis algorithm** in words and code. 3. Explain the roles of irreducibility, aperiodicity, and stationarity. 4. Use traceplots and acceptance rates to recognize obvious problems. 5. Explain burn-in and why starting values can matter. 6. Describe how MCMC can be used to break a substitution cipher. ## Motivation ![](https://sta101.github.io/static/img/prisonLetter.png){width="75%"} [Diaconis, Persi. "The Markov chain Monte Carlo revolution." Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 46.2 (2009): 179-205.](https://math.uchicago.edu/~shmuel/Network-course-readings/MCMCRev.pdf) ## Basic cryptology terminology - cryptography: making secret messages (encryption) - substitution - transposition - cryptanalysis: breaking secret messages (decryption) - cryptology: the study of cryptography and cryptanalysis . . . - plain text: the actual message - cipher text: the encrypted message - key: information to encode (or decode) cryptographic key - symmetric (same key for encryption and decryption) - asymmetric (different key to encrypt and decrypt) ## Substitution cipher - Idea: each character of plaintext is substituted with another character . . . Example: ![](images/ex-rot13.png){fig-align="center" width="600"} From ## Brute force approach? - Trying every possible key is known as a "brute force" approach. . . . Since every key is a permutation of the alphabet, there are $$ 26! $$ possible keys. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} factorial(26) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.032915e+26 ``` ::: ::: If you're computer could "try" 1 million keys per second, it would still take 4.6677252\times 10^{15} years to try every possible key and guarantee a solution. . . . - Chat with your neighbor and develop a strategy better than the brute force approach. ## Some keys are much better than others Suppose one candidate key produces ```text THERE IS NO WAR IN BA SING SE ``` and another produces ```text ZITKT OL FG CQK OF WQ LOFU LT ``` The first looks much more like English. We can create a numerical score: $$ S(\text{key}) = \text{how English-like is the decoded text?} $$ Higher score = more plausible key. ## Instead of searching every key We could: 1. Start with one candidate key. 2. Make a **small random change**. 3. Decode the message. 4. Compare the new score with the current score. 5. Decide whether to move to the new key. 6. Repeat. This creates a sequence of candidate keys. . . . If the moves in "key space" are only based on the current position, the sequence will be a **Markov chain**. ## Recall: the Markov property A Markov chain is a sequence $$ X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots $$ where the next state depends on the current state: $$ P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\ldots) = P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t). $$ For cryptanalysis, $$ X_t = \text{candidate key at iteration } t. $$ ## Recall: stationary distributions For a long Markov chain, the fraction of time spent in state $j$ can estimate its stationary probability: $$ \widehat{\pi}_j = \frac{\text{number of visits to state }j} {\text{number of iterations}}. $$ This suggests a powerful idea: > What if we construct a chain whose stationary distribution favors the states > we want to find? ## Markov chain Monte Carlo **Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** means: > Construct a Markov chain whose long-run distribution is a distribution we > want to explore. Then use the states visited by the chain as simulated draws. For cryptanalysis, we want: - high-scoring keys visited often, - low-scoring keys visited rarely. ## A target distribution Suppose every possible state $x$ has a nonnegative score $$ f(x). $$ We want stationary probabilities proportional to those scores: $$ \pi(x) \propto f(x). $$ The symbol $\propto$ means **proportional to**. We do not need to know the constant that makes all the probabilities sum to 1. ## Why proportional is enough Suppose $$ \pi(x) = \frac{f(x)}{C} $$ for some unknown constant $C$. Then $$ \frac{\pi(x^\star)}{\pi(x)} = \frac{f(x^\star)}{f(x)}. $$ The unknown constant cancels. That is one reason MCMC is useful when a target is easy to **score** but hard to sample from directly. ## One Metropolis step Suppose the chain is currently at $x$. 1. Propose a nearby state $x^\star$. 2. Calculate $$ r = \frac{f(x^\star)}{f(x)}. $$ 3. Accept the proposal with probability $$ \min(1,r). $$ Otherwise, remain at $x$. ## Why accept worse proposals? If $f(x^\star) > f(x)$, then $r>1$, so the proposal is always accepted. If $f(x^\star) < f(x)$, it can still be accepted. For example, if $$ r=0.8, $$ we accept the worse proposal with probability $0.8$. If we accepted only improvements, we could become trapped at a local optimum. ## The Metropolis algorithm in R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (t in 2:n_steps) { proposal <- propose(current) ratio <- target_score(proposal) / target_score(current) accept_prob <- min(1, ratio) if (runif(1) < accept_prob) { current <- proposal } chain[t] <- current } ``` ::: After a rejection, `current` does not change. ## A note on numerical stability Practically, we want to avoid computing ``` ratio <- target_score(proposal) / target_score(current) ``` directly, because it could be numerically unstable for very small/large `target_score()`. To make things more stable, we always `log` the ratio and modify the code as such: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (t in 2:n_steps) { proposal <- propose(current) log_ratio <- log_target_score(proposal) - log_target_score(current) if (log(runif(1)) < log_ratio) { current <- proposal } chain[t] <- current } ``` ::: ## A simple target Before returning to cryptanalysis, consider $$ f(x) = \exp\left[ -\frac{1}{2} \left({x-10}\right)^2 \right]. $$ ::: panel-tabset ## Plot ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(x = seq(-3, 9, length.out = 300)) |> ggplot(aes(x = x)) + stat_function(fun = target_score, linewidth = 1) + labs( y = "Target score", title = "Where should the chain spend its time?" ) ``` ::: ::: The target is largest near $x=10$. ## Propose a nearby state Use a random step around the current position: $$ X^\star \sim N(X_t,\sigma^2). $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} proposal <- rnorm( 1, mean = current, sd = proposal_sd ) ``` ::: This is a **random-walk proposal**. ## A complete Metropolis function ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(323) metropolis <- function(n_steps = 5000, start = 0, proposal_sd = 1) { theta_s = start # starting point THETA = NULL # empty object to save iterations in S = n_steps # number of iterations delta = proposal_sd # proposal sd accept = 0 # keep track of acceptance rate ACCEPTED = NULL for (s in 1:S) { accepted <- FALSE # log everything for numerical stability # ### generate proposal and compute ratio r ### theta_proposal = rnorm(1, mean = theta_s, sd = delta) log.r = dnorm(theta_proposal, mean = 10, sd = 1, log = TRUE) - dnorm(theta_s, mean = 10, sd = 1, log = TRUE) ### accept or reject proposal and add to chain ### if (log(runif(1)) < log.r) { theta_s = theta_proposal accepted = TRUE } THETA = c(THETA, theta_s) ACCEPTED <- c(ACCEPTED, accepted) } tibble(iteration = 1:n_steps, THETA, accepted = ACCEPTED) } ``` ::: ## Run the chain ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chain <- metropolis( n_steps = 5000, start = -3, proposal_sd = 1 ) chain ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5,000 × 3 iteration THETA accepted 1 1 -3 FALSE 2 2 -3 FALSE 3 3 -2.78 TRUE 4 4 -2.56 TRUE 5 5 -2.42 TRUE 6 6 -2.33 TRUE 7 7 -1.94 TRUE 8 8 -1.94 FALSE 9 9 -1.80 TRUE 10 10 -1.93 TRUE # ℹ 4,990 more rows ``` ::: ::: These simulations are **dependent**. Each state was generated using the previous state. The hope is that their long-run distribution is still the target distribution. ## Choose delta We have to choose $\delta$. How should we choose it? Let's gain some intuition by trying out three different values of $\delta$. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Let's look at how various $\delta$ let us sample the target: ::: panel-tabset ## $\delta = 0.1$ ## $\delta = 1$ ## $\delta = 4$ ::: ## Trace plots Let's look at the trace plots for each $\delta$. A **traceplot** shows the state of the chain against iteration. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: panel-tabset ## delta = 0.1 ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## delta = 1 ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## delta = 4 ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Acceptance rate for each delta | 0.1| 1| 4| |----:|---:|----:| | 0.96| 0.7| 0.29| ::: ::: ::: ## Intuition: blind monkey on an island :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/monkey.png){width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/pond.png){width="100%"} ::: :::: ## Stationary does not automatically mean convergence A distribution $\pi$ is stationary if $$ \pi = \pi P. $$ But a chain must also be able to explore its state space properly. Two important properties are: - **irreducible:** every state can eventually be reached from every other state, - **aperiodic:** the chain is not forced to revisit states only at regularly spaced times. These conditions prevent important ways a chain can fail to explore. ## Why Metropolis often gives aperiodicity When a Metropolis proposal is rejected, $$ X_{t+1}=X_t. $$ The chain can remain in the same state. For an irreducible chain, the ability to stay put is a simple way to obtain aperiodicity. So rejection is not merely wasted computation, it is part of the Markov chain we intentionally construct to guarantee aperiodicity. ## The practical convergence story For the chains we use, we want: - the desired stationary distribution, - the ability to reach all relevant regions, - no forced cyclic behavior. Then, after running long enough, $$ \text{distribution of }X_t \longrightarrow \pi. $$ Long-run averages from the chain can then approximate averages under $\pi$. ::: {.callout-note} There are more technical conditions behind MCMC convergence. Here we focus on the computational intuition and practical warning signs. ::: ## Starting values and burn-in Our chain deliberately started far from the center of the target. Early iterations can therefore reflect the arbitrary starting value. A common strategy is to discard an initial portion: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} burn_in <- 500 chain_kept <- chain |> filter(iteration > burn_in) ``` ::: This discarded portion is called **burn-in** or **warm-up**. There is no universal correct number of iterations to discard. ## Did we reach the target? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chain_kept |> ggplot(aes(x = THETA)) + geom_histogram( aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40 ) + stat_function( fun = function(x) dnorm(x, mean = 10, sd = 1), linewidth = 1 ) + labs( x = "x", y = "Density", title = "MCMC draws after warm-up" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: The histogram should approximately follow the target shape. ## Acceptance rate The **acceptance rate** is the fraction of proposed moves that were accepted. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(chain$accepted) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7012 ``` ::: ::: Very low acceptance can mean the chain is repeatedly proposing moves that are too large. Very high acceptance can occur when proposed moves are so small that the chain moves only very slowly. ## Mixing A chain **mixes well** when it moves efficiently through the important parts of the target distribution. Warning signs of poor mixing include: - long flat stretches, - very slow wandering, - important regions visited only rarely. No single plot or statistic proves that a chain has mixed well. ## Multiple starting values Run several chains from very different places: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} starts <- c(-8, 0, 8, 15) chains <- map_dfr( starts, function(s) { metropolis( n_steps = 2500, start = s, proposal_sd = 1 ) |> mutate(start = factor(s)) } ) ``` ::: If all chains eventually explore the same region, that is reassuring. ## Compare the chains ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chains |> ggplot( aes( x = iteration, y = THETA, group = start ) ) + geom_line(alpha = .6) + facet_wrap(~ start, ncol = 1) + labs( x = "Iteration", y = "State" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-mcmc_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: If chains started in different places remain in completely different regions, we may be concerned. ## Back to cryptanalysis: the state and proposal For the substitution cipher, $$ X_t = \text{current substitution key}. $$ A simple proposal is: > Pick two letters at random and swap their assignments. Any permutation can be transformed into any other permutation through a sequence of swaps. So this proposal can, in principle, reach every possible key. That gives us **irreducibility**. ## Score the decoded message We need a score that rewards English-looking text. One approach uses frequencies of neighboring letters. Common patterns such as ```text TH HE IN ER AN ``` receive higher scores than unusual patterns such as ```text QZ ZX JQ ``` Combine these contributions across the decoded message to obtain an **English log-score**. ## Acceptance using log scores Suppose the current and proposed log-scores are $$ \ell \quad\text{and}\quad \ell^\star. $$ The score ratio is $$ \exp(\ell^\star-\ell). $$ So accept the proposed key with probability $$ \min\left(1,\exp(\ell^\star-\ell)\right). $$ A better decoding is always accepted; a worse decoding sometimes is. ## Cryptanalysis pseudocode ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} current_key <- initial_key current_score <- score(decode(ciphertext, current_key)) for (t in 2:n_steps) { proposed_key <- swap_two_letters(current_key) proposed_score <- score(decode(ciphertext, proposed_key)) accept_prob <- min( 1, exp(proposed_score - current_score) ) if (runif(1) < accept_prob) { current_key <- proposed_key current_score <- proposed_score } chain[[t]] <- current_key scores[t] <- current_score } ``` ::: ## Try it yourself ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} download.file(url = "https://sta323-fa26.github.io/scripts/cryptanalysis.qmd", destfile = "cryptanalysis.qmd") ``` ::: ## What should we plot? The state is a 26-letter permutation, so a direct traceplot of the state is not useful. Instead, plot the **English score**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( iteration = 1:n_steps, score = scores ) |> ggplot(aes(iteration, score)) + geom_line() ``` ::: We want to see the chain reach and continue exploring high-scoring keys. ## Diagnostics for the cipher chain Useful checks include: - **Traceplot:** does the English score settle into a high-scoring region? - **Acceptance rate:** are nearly all swaps rejected? - **Multiple starts:** do different random keys find similar decryptions? - **Best decoded text:** does it actually look like English? - **Longer run:** does running longer materially change the result? For cryptanalysis, the decoded text itself is an unusually useful diagnostic. ## Burn-in for the cipher A random starting key usually decodes to nonsense. The beginning of the chain mostly describes its trip away from that arbitrary starting key. We may discard an initial section: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kept_scores <- scores[-(1:burn_in)] kept_keys <- chain[-(1:burn_in)] ``` ::: The traceplot should help us judge whether the early behavior looks different from the later behavior. ## MCMC or optimization? For cryptanalysis, we may care most about the **best key found**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best_iteration <- which.max(scores) best_key <- chain[[best_iteration]] ``` ::: So this application has an optimization flavor. But MCMC's defining goal is broader: > Construct a chain with a chosen stationary distribution and use its visited > states for Monte Carlo calculations. ## Why this is Monte Carlo Once the chain is exploring its stationary distribution, we can estimate an average under the target using $$ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^N h(X_t). $$ This looks like ordinary Monte Carlo. The key difference is: > The simulated values are dependent because they come from a Markov chain. Hence: > **Markov chain Monte Carlo** ## References - Diaconis, P. (2009). "The Markov chain Monte Carlo revolution." *Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society*, 46(2), 179--205. - Metropolis, N., Rosenbluth, A. W., Rosenbluth, M. N., Teller, A. H., & Teller, E. (1953). "Equation of state calculations by fast computing machines." *Journal of Chemical Physics*, 21, 1087--1092.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
